material.name: HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy
material.form: gas atomized powder with low oxygen content

intervention.description: SPS treatment of gas atomized powder

structure.description: Specimen with refined microstructure after subsequent deformation
microstructure: very fine microstructure with grain size well below 500 nm

evidence_units.mechanism: Microstructure can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation
evidence_spans: The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 500 nm.
Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen.

intervention.action: Sintering, hot isostatic pressing, and swaging
intervention.description: Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy

evidence_units.mechanism: The method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging
evidence_spans: Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging.

evidence_units.mechanism: hot compression deformation eliminates residual porosity
evidence_spans: Our previous experiments showed that the residual porosity of as-sintered HfNbTaTiZr specimens was eliminated during hot compression tests.
However, it should be pointed out that the hot compression tests and real forging processes may significantly differ from each other.
limitations: hot compression tests and real forging processes may significantly differ from each other

material.name: HEAP green compact
material.composition: HfNbTaTiZr alloy (Nb and Ta powders bcc; Hf, Ti, Zr elements hcp)

structure.description: Multiple phases: bcc (Nb, Ta) and hcp (Hf, Ti, Zr).
defects: vacancy-like misfit defects at interfaces between precipitates and matrix

evidence_units.mechanism: Positrons trapped at vacancy-like misfit defects at interfaces and at dislocations introduced by CIP; dislocation density calculated using two-state trapping model assuming τ2 arises exclusively from dislocations (upper level estimate).

outcome.measurement_method: two-state trapping model from LT lifetime τ2 ≈ 165 ps

evidence_spans: The HEAP green compacts exhibited an oxygen concentration of ≈0.55 wt %.
The sample contained the bcc (Nb and Ta powders have both the bcc lattice with similar parameters) and hcp phases (Hf, Ti, and Zr elements).

Assuming that the component τ 2 arose exclusively from positrons trapped at dislocations, the mean dislocation density ρ D ≈ 1.48 × 10 14 m −2 in the sample could be calculated from the two-state trapping model [ [37] ].
This value should be considered as an upper level of the actual dislocation density in the sample since some fraction of positrons contributing to the component τ 2 was trapped at misfit defects.
limitations: value should be considered an upper level of actual dislocation density since some positrons trapped at misfit defects

material.name: AT powder
material.initial_state: dendritic structure with two chemically different bcc phases

intervention.description: Production of coarse powder in protective Ar atmosphere

structure.description: Dendritic structure with two bcc phases: bcc1 (Nb, Ta rich) and bcc2 (Hf, Zr rich).
defects: misfit defects at interfaces between bcc1 and bcc2 phases

evidence_units.mechanism: Discontinuity of lattice planes between bcc1 and bcc2 phases with slightly different lattice parameters results in formation of misfit defects at interfaces; positrons trapped at these misfit defects.

outcome.measurement_method: not explicitly stated as quantitative comparison value, but described as ten times lower

evidence_spans: One can see in Figure 1 b that the AT particles exhibited a dendritic structure typical for conventionally cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy [ [39] ] and consisted of two chemically different phases with bcc structures: one bcc phase, denoted bcc1, was slightly rich in Nb and Ta, and the second bcc phase, denoted bcc2, was rich in Hf, Zr.
Since bcc1 and bcc2 phases had slightly different lattice parameters, the discontinuity of lattice planes resulted in the formation of misfit defects at interfaces between these two phases [ [27] ].
AT powder exhibited a single component LT spectrum with a lifetime of ≈165 ps. It represented a contribution of positrons trapped at misfit defects at the interfaces between bcc1 and bcc2 phases.

AT powder exhibited low oxygen content (ten times lower than MA) since crucible-free gas atomization was performed in a protective Ar atmosphere and particles of AT powder were rather coarse, i.e., the surface-to-volume ration was relatively low.

structure.description: Nanocrystalline structure with broad XRD reflections.

evidence_units.mechanism: High surface area of nanocrystalline powder particles leads to oxygen incorporation during high energy ball milling.
evidence_spans: The sample exhibited very broad XRD reflections at positions corresponding to the bcc phase with lattice parameter a = 3.409(1) Å, which was slightly higher than that for the AT powder. Broad XRD reflections testified that MA powder had a nanocrystalline structure.
The average size of coherently scattering domains determined by Rietveld refinement was 22.7(6) nm.

The MA powder exhibited rather high oxygen content of ≈1.07 wt %, which was ten times higher than that in the AT powder. Oxygen was incorporated into the MA powder obviously during high energy ball milling due to high surface area of nanocrystalline powder particles. Note that LT investigations of nanocrystalline MA powder were not performed because of its high reactivity with oxygen.
limitations: LT investigations of nanocrystalline MA powder were not performed because of its high reactivity with oxygen

intervention.description: Hot swaging to remove residual porosity

structure.description: Similar to HEAP-S; radial cracks observed.

evidence_units.mechanism: Brittleness caused by relatively high oxygen content (~0.75 wt %) at given deformation conditions; dislocations introduced by swaging strengthen material; cracking during swaging may affect hardness measurement.

conditions.temperature: hot swaging (temperature not explicitly stated, noted as potentially too low)
conditions.strain_rate: not stated (noted as potentially too high)

evidence_spans: The as-sintered specimen (HEAP-S) was hot swaged to remove residual porosity.
However, the swaging process was not completed due to cracking of the specimens, which can be clearly seen in Figure 5 .

It should be pointed out that this specimen contained relatively high amount of oxygen (~0.75 wt %), which may have caused the brittleness of this alloy at the given deformation conditions (i.e., temperature and strain rate).
It is also possible that the deformation temperature was too low and the strain rate was too high for the given specimens.
Table 2 shows that hardness increased during hot swaging to more than 400 HV10, indicating strengthening of the material by dislocations introduced by swaging.
A significant increase of dislocation density up to ≈3 × 10 14 m −2 in the swaged sample was confirmed by LT spectroscopy, as seen in Table 3 .
However, it should be accentuated that the specimen was damaged during swaging and therefore this hardness value may not be representative.
limitations: hardness value may not be representative due to cracks opening under indent

material.name: AT-SPS
material.initial_state: equiaxed microstructure with pure bcc phase

structure.description: Highly deformed; mean grain size decreased below 0.5 μm; equiaxed microstructure.

evidence_units.mechanism: HPT processing results in saturated positron trapping in dislocations; high density of dislocations formed.

outcome.measurement_method: LT spectroscopy (saturated positron trapping, τ 2 ≈ 180 ps)

evidence_spans: The AT-SPS-HPT sample had an equiaxed microstructure with a pure bcc phase and the lattice parameter a = 3.406(4) Å. No residual porosity and no precipitates of secondary phases were observed, as seen in Figure 7 .
The mean grain size of sample AT-SPS (i.e., before HPT straining) was ≈50 μm, as seen in Figure 7 .
After HPT deformation (sample AT-SPS-HPT), the mean grain size decreased below 0.5 μm.
The microstructure was highly deformed.
One can see in Table 3 that both MA-SPS-HPT and AT-SPS-HPT samples exhibited a single component LT spectrum with lifetime τ 2 ≈ 180 ps.
This testifies that virtually all positrons were annihilated in a trapped state in dislocations (so called saturated positron trapping).
Hence, one can conclude that HPT processing resulted in formation of a high density of dislocations exceeding 5 × 10 14 m −2 .

structure.description: Equiaxed very fine (grain size ~4 μm) microstructure with numerous precipitates and some amount of porosity; damaged with cracks.

evidence_units.mechanism: HPT processing results in saturated positron trapping in dislocations; high density of dislocations formed; oxygen introduced during MA processing.

outcome.measurement_method: LT spectroscopy (saturated positron trapping, τ 2 ≈ 180 ps)

evidence_spans: The microstructure of the MA-SPS-HPT specimen consisted of an equiaxed very fine (grain size ~4 μm) microstructure with numerous precipitates and some amount of porosity (see Figure 6 ).
It should be accentuated that the MA-SPS specimen was damaged during the HPT process, as many cracks emerged, and the specimen was separated into several smaller pieces.

material.name: HEAP
material.initial_state: MA powder compacted by SPS containing residual porosity

intervention.description: HIP processing applied to decrease residual porosity

structure.description: Considerable porosity remained in the specimen

evidence_units.mechanism: High volume fraction of pores and filling of pores by Ar gas used as a pressing medium prevented complete removal of porosity
evidence_spans: Results obtained for HEAP-S and HEAP-S-HIP samples (see Table 2 ) indicate that HIP processing had some potential to decrease residual porosity. However, this decrease was quite small and considerable porosity remained in the specimen. The fact that even HIP processing at 1400 °C/200 MPa/2 h did not remove the porosity completely can be ascribed to a high volume fraction of pores and to filling of the pores by Ar gas used as a pressing medium in HIP processing.

intervention.description: SPS processing applied to AT powder

evidence_units.mechanism: relatively high cooling rate after SPS processing at high temperature of 1300 °C dissolved all secondary phases
evidence_spans: Contrary to this, SPS processing at 1300 °C of AT powder resulted in porosity-free samples (see Figure 7 ).

The AT-SPS is the only sample with single phase bcc solid solution with no other phases. Single phase random solid solution is caused by relatively high cooling rate after SPS processing at high temperature of 1300 °C, where all secondary phases are supposed to be dissolved

The cooling rate after SPS is very high as the sample was cooled from sintering temperature (1300 °C) to room temperature in 3–4 min. Therefore the achieved cooling rate around 300 °C/min is much higher than 15 °C/min.

It also seems that the oxygen content was decisive for the plasticity of the alloy as the only specimen with enough ductility to undergo the cold plastic deformation was the AT-SPS specimen, which had the lowest oxygen content.

intervention.description: HPT straining applied to MA-SPS specimen

structure.description: high number of nucleation sites for new grains

evidence_units.mechanism: intensive plastic deformation during high energy ball milling resulted in a high number of nucleation sites; dislocations introduced by severe cold plastic deformation; presence of oxide particles caused additional strengthening
evidence_spans: Very high hardness of the MA-SPS-HPT specimen (584 HV10) can be ascribed to the high oxygen content in solid solution and also the presence of oxide particles that caused additional strengthening.

As seen in Figure 8 hardness was correlated with oxygen content in the sample. Hardness remained approximately unchanged with increasing oxygen content up to the oxygen concentration of ≈0.8 wt %. Above this value hardness strongly increased with oxygen concentration.

It is likely that the remarkable hardening effect of oxygen above 0.8 wt % was connected with the formation of HfO 2 particles with a monoclinic structure, which were detected in MA-SPS and MA-SPS-HPT samples by SEM and X-ray diffraction.
Additional strengthening (not connected with oxygen) was caused by dislocations introduced by severe (cold) plastic deformation.

The grain size of the MA-SPS specimen was lower than for the others (except that after HPT). This was caused by the intensive plastic deformation during high energy ball milling, which resulted in a high number of nucleation sites for new grains formed by recrystallization during SPS processing.
In Figure 8 one can see that HPT straining increased hardness of both MA-SPS-HPT and AT-SPS-HPT samples.

intervention.description: subsequent sintering applied to HEAP-HIP sample

evidence_units.mechanism: improved chemical homogeneity; partial formation of random solid solution
evidence_spans: It has to be mentioned that HEAP-HIP and HEAP-HIP-S samples were characterized by surprisingly low hardness. Hardness measurement of these samples could be influenced by porosity. Moreover, the low hardness of the HEAP-HIP sample could be possibly attributed to different phase composition.
One can see in Figure 4 c that Ta and Nb rich particles were not fully dissolved during HIP and therefore this specimen was somewhat between a blend of powders and a high entropy alloy.
This was proved also by the XRD pattern in Figure 2 , which showed the highest difference between lattice parameters of the bcc1 and bcc2 phases.

Subsequent sintering improved the chemical homogeneity of the HEAP-HIP sample and increased hardness as well. However, the hardness of HEAP-HIP-S still did not reach the values of HEAP-S and HEAP-S-HIP.
limitations: hardness still did not reach values of HEAP-S and HEAP-S-HIP

structure.description: Equiaxed and relatively fine grains; good chemical homogeneity; secondary phases (needle-like precipitates) and irregular shaped particles of hcp phase.

candidate.mechanism: Grain growth during sintering reduces dislocation density and concentration of misfit defects; sintering leads to increase of bcc2 phase concentration at expense of bcc1.

conditions.temperature: not explicitly stated for sintering step alone (later step 1400°C mentioned for HEAP-HIP-S)

evidence_spans: Sintering resulted in equiaxed and relatively fine grains. The chemical homogeneity was good after 16 h sintering as determined by SEM and EDS microstructure analysis.
The sintering caused narrowing of XRD profiles, which indicated grain growth occurring during sintering.

LT investigations revealed that sintering reduced dislocation density and also the concentration of misfit defects, which was indicated by increases of τ 2 towards the value of ≈180 ps, typical for dislocations in HfNbTaTiZr alloy [ [38] ].
The latter effect was obviously caused by grain growth during sintering.

structure.description: Chemical inhomogeneities (areas with higher Ta or Nb concentration); bcc1, bcc2, and hcp phases present.

candidate.mechanism: Elements not fully dissolved during HIP of green powders leads to chemical inhomogeneities; HIP introduces dislocations.
evidence_spans: HIP processing of sintered specimens (HEAP-S-HIP) introduced no significant changes.
The microstructure of green compact subjected to HIP treatment (HEAP-HIP) is shown in Figure 4 c,d.
Several chemical inhomogeneities (i.e., areas with higher Ta, or Nb concentration-probably at the positions of original Ta particles) were observed in the HEAP-HIP sample.
The HIP process caused a slight decrease in porosity, but the specimens still remained rather porous, as seen in Figure 4 c.
Interestingly the hardness of the HEAP-HIP specimen was around 150 HV10, which was significantly lower value than that of HEAP-S.
The HIP treatment of sintered sample led to a slight increase of dislocation density, as seen in Table 3 , due to dislocations introduced by HIP processing.
